A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DDSPO research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: V1 reports original two-dimensional simulations, image-generation evaluations, ablations and qualitative comparisons in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds supervised DDSPO evaluations, human judgments, generation-seed analyses, alternative-method comparisons and computational measurements.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 adds DD-CPP: separately training winning and losing diffusion models on preferred and dispreferred images, then using their predictions as DDSPO targets. This introduces a substantial training procedure beyond v1's prompt-conditioned reference model. The original objective and prompt-based implementation, renamed TF-CPP, remain.

E1.justification: DDSPO training expands to actual Pick-a-Pic preference image pairs through DD-CPP. V1 used Pick-a-Pic through supervised comparators and qualitative prompts, while training DDSPO on generated pairs. The alignment and aesthetic tasks and existing evaluation datasets remain; the additional backbones principally change experimental settings.

E2.justification: V2 Appendix C adds directly evaluated SoftREPA and a CFG-style target-regression baseline. It also evaluates SPO for text-image alignment, whereas v1's reported SPO comparison concerned aesthetics. These additions substantially broaden comparison with competing annotation-free and stepwise approaches. SoftREPA was already cited in v1 but was not evaluated there.

E3.justification: V2 adds SD3-Medium and SD3.5-Large configurations, supervised policy-pair training, and a blinded human-evaluation protocol with 15 annotators judging 30 prompt-matched pairs. New analyses introduce a 1,000-prompt CLIP/LAION evaluation and controlled hardware timing. Existing TF-CPP training settings are largely retained; these are predominantly new experimental protocols.

E4.justification: V2 adds tests of whether fixed CFG-style target regression explains TF-CPP, quantifies training/evaluation distribution mismatch using FID, measures effective prompt-degradation strength, and benchmarks computational overhead. It also examines SPO's alignment failures. Existing dataset-size, beta, prompt-strategy, negative-image and joint-objective analyses are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: V1 reports point estimates without repeated-evaluation uncertainty. V2 Table D adds means and standard deviations over five generation seeds for aesthetic comparisons on two backbones, keeping checkpoints fixed. Timing measurements are averaged over 30 microbatches after five warmups. This is a limited extension of uncertainty reporting, not evidence of repeated training runs.

E6.justification: Original Table 1 and prompt-based DDSPO scores are largely retained. V2 Table 3 adds Pick-a-Pic-trained DDSPO results: HPSv2/PickScore of 27.60/21.50 on SD-1.5 and 29.09/22.71 on SDXL. Additional backbone, comparator, degradation and timing results substantially expand the evidence. Figure C newly reports overall human preferences of 42.9% for DDSPO, 36.0% for Diffusion-DPO and 21.1% ties.

T1.justification: Appendix A corrects losing-branch distribution arguments in Equations (19) and (28), replacing incorrectly used winning variables with losing variables and restoring a losing-policy superscript. The core mathematical objectives and derivation structure remain; no substantial new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden the contribution from a practical label-free approach to a framework with supervised DD-CPP and label-free TF-CPP. They also recenter the principal claim on backward-transition policy supervision versus forward-process targets. Claims about avoiding preference labels now apply specifically to TF-CPP.

C2.justification: V1's limitation that final-output preferences cannot directly support its practical method is replaced by discussion of policy-pair quality and construction cost. V2 adds explanations distinguishing pairwise optimization from fixed-target regression and relating degradation strength to downstream performance. It also explicitly acknowledges that D-KTO and SPO outperform DDSPO on some aesthetic metrics.

D1.justification: V2 adds an implementation-access link and substantial configuration details for DD-CPP and the new backbones. Appendix D specifies policy-training LoRA rank, learning rate, checkpoint selection and beta, plus timing hardware, precision and measurement procedures. The earlier approximate overhead statement is supplemented by measured costs; existing SDXL generation and training resource estimates remain.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to Christiano et al., Ouyang et al. and the SD3 rectified-flow work. It expands discussion of the already cited SoftREPA and refines distinctions from Diffusion-DPO and SPO. The broader literature coverage and related-work organization remain largely intact.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract, contribution narrative, practical-method exposition, conclusion and limitations around DD-CPP and TF-CPP. It consolidates v1's separate joint-objective and dataset-size appendix sections into extended results and introduces a dedicated alternative-comparison section. These changes materially reorganize the narrative beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: V2 changes the main text from two columns to one, merges v1 Tables 2/3 and 5/6, and splits the aesthetic table by backbone. It reorganizes qualitative displays, including moving earlier appendix examples into Figure 2. New displays include the human-preference chart, additional comparison tables and a DD-CPP image gallery; many existing plots and images are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's explicit restriction concerning final-output preference data by implementing and evaluating DD-CPP. Pick-a-Pic-trained comparisons, blinded human judgments, generation-seed uncertainty and targeted mechanism analyses substantially strengthen validation beyond v1's automatic scores. Added implementation and cost details improve reproducibility. The new SD3-M CompBench comparison has an aggregation inconsistency between Table 2b and its stated protocol, limiting that comparison, but this does not outweigh the substantial gains in applicability and supporting evidence.
